{{Short description|Mathematical object}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''random polytope''' is a structure commonly used in [[convex analysis]]  and the analysis of [[Linear programming|linear programs]] in ''d''-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^d</math>.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=May |first1=Jerrold H. |last2=Smith |first2=Robert L. |title=Random polytopes: Their definition, generation and aggregate properties |journal=Mathematical Programming |date=December 1982 |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=39–54 |doi=10.1007/BF01585093|hdl=2027.42/47911 |s2cid=17838156 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Depending on use the construction and definition, random polytopes may differ.
[[File:RandomPoltyope(1).png|thumb|Random polytope of a set of random points in accordance with definition 1]]

== Definition ==

There are multiple non equivalent definitions of a Random polytope. For the following definitions. Let ''K'' be a bounded [[Convex set|convex]] set in a [[Euclidean space]]:
* The convex hull of random points selected with respect to a uniform distribution inside K.<ref name=":0" />
* The nonempty intersection of [[half-space (geometry)|half-space]]s in <math>\R^d</math>.<ref name=":1" />
** The following parameterization has been used: <math>r:(\R^d \times \{0,1\})^m\rightarrow \text{Polytopes} \in \R^d</math> such that <math>r((p_1, 0), (p_2, 1), (p_3, 1)...(p_m, i_m)) = \{x \in \R^n: | \frac{p_j}{||p_j||} \cdot x \leq ||p_j|| \text{ if } i_j=1,  \frac{p_j}{||p_j||} \cdot x \geq ||p_j|| \text{ if } i_j=0 \}</math> (Note: these polytopes can be empty).<ref name=":1" />

=== Properties definition 1 === <!--If there is a more accepted name insert it here per WP:COMMONNAME-->
Let <math>\Kappa </math> be the set of convex bodies in <math>\R^d</math>. Assume <math>K \in\Kappa </math> and consider a set of [[Continuous uniform distribution|uniformly distributed]] points <math>x_1, ..., x_n</math> in <math>K </math>. The [[convex hull]] of these points, <math>K_n </math>, is called a random polytope inscribed in <math>K </math>. <math>K_n = [x_1, ..., x_n] </math> where the set <math>[S] </math> stands for the [[convex hull]] of the set.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |chapter=Random Polytopes, Convex Bodies, and Approximation |date=2007 |title=Stochastic Geometry: Lectures given at the C.I.M.E. Summer School held in Martina Franca, Italy, September 13–18, 2004 |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |volume=1892 |pages=77–118 |editor-last=Baddeley |editor-first=Adrian |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-38175-4_2 |isbn=978-3-540-38175-4 |editor2-last=Bárány |editor2-first=Imre | editor2-link=Imre Bárány |editor3-last=Schneider |editor3-first=Rolf |editor4-last=Weil |editor4-first=Wolfgang|editor4-link=Wolfgang Weil (mathematician) }}</ref> We define <math>E(k,n)</math> to be the expected volume of <math>K - K_n</math>. For a large enough <math>n</math> and given <math>K \in \R^n</math>.

* vol <math>K(\frac{1}{n})\ll E(K,n) \ll</math> vol <math>K(\frac{1}{n})</math><ref name=":0" />
** Note: One can determine the volume of the wet part to obtain the order of the magnitude of <math>E(K,n) </math>, instead of determining <math>E(K,n)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bárány |first1=I. |author-link1=Imre Bárány |last2=Larman |first2=D. G. |title=Convex bodies, economic cap coverings, random polytopes |journal=[[Mathematika]] |date=December 1988 |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=274–291 |doi=10.1112/S0025579300015266}}</ref>
* For the [[unit ball]] <math>B^d \in \R^d</math>, the wet part <math>B^d(v \leq t)</math> is the [[Annulus (mathematics)|annulus]] <math>\frac{B^d}{(1-h)B^d}</math> where h is of order <math>t^{\frac{2}{d+1}}</math>: <math>E(B^d,n) \approx </math> vol <math>B^d (\frac{1}{n}) \approx n^{\frac{-2}{d+1}}</math><ref name=":0" />

Given we have <math>V = V(x_1,...,x_d)</math> is the volume of a smaller cap cut off from <math>K</math> by aff<math>(x_1,...,x_d)</math>, and <math>F=[x_1,...,x_d]</math> is a facet if and only if <math>x_{d+1},...,x_n</math> are all on one side of aff <math>\{x_1,...,x_d\}</math>.

* <math>E_{\phi}(K_n) = {{n}\choose{d}} \int_K ... \int_K [(1-V)^{n-d} + V^{n-d}]\phi(F)dx_1...dx_d</math>.<ref name=":0" />
** Note: If <math>\phi = f_{d-1}</math> (a function that returns the amount of d-1 dimensional faces), then <math>\phi(F) = 1</math> and formula can be evaluated for smooth convex sets and for polygons in the plane. 
<!--The following is true for smooth convex sets of area equal to 1: *<math>E_{f_1}(K_n) = \biggl(\frac{2}{3}\biggr)^{\frac{1}{3}}\gamma\biggl(\frac{5}{3}\biggr)\biggl(\int_{bd(K)}\kappa^{\frac{1}{3}}ds\biggr) n^{\frac{1}{3}}(1+o(1))</math><ref name=":0" />
**Note: <math>\kappa</math> is the curvature and integration is by arc length <math>ds</math> on the boundary <math>bd(K)</math> of the convex body.-->

=== Properties definition 2 === <!--If there is a more accepted name insert it here per WP:COMMONNAME-->
Assume we are given a [[Multivariate normal distribution|multivariate]] [[probability distribution]] on <math>(\R^d \times \{ 0, 1\})^m=(p_1\times i_1,\dots,p_m\times i_m)^m</math> that is

# Absolutely continuous on <math>(p_1,\dots,p_d)</math> with respect to [[Lebesgue measure|Lebesgue]] measure.
# Generates either 0 or 1 for the <math>i</math>s with probability of <math>\frac{1}{2}</math> each.
# Assigns a measure of 0 to the set of elements in <math>(\R^d \times \{ 0, 1\})^m</math> that correspond to empty polytopes.

Given this distribution, and our assumptions, the following properties hold:

* A formula is derived for the expected number of <math>k</math> dimensional faces on a polytope in <math>\R^d</math> with <math>m</math> constraints: <math>E_k(m) = 2^{d-k} \sum_{i = d - k}^{d}{{i}\choose{d-k}}{{m}\choose{i}}/\sum_{i=0}^{d}{{m}\choose{i}}</math>. (Note: <math>\lim_{m \to \infty}E_k(m) = {{d}\choose{d-k}}2^{d-k}</math> where <math>m>d</math>). The upper bound, or worst case, for the number of vertices with <math>m</math> constraints is much larger: <math>V_{max} = {m-[\frac{1}{2}(d+1)]\choose m-d} + {m-[\frac{1}{2}(d+2)]\choose m-d}</math>.<ref name=":1" />
* The probability that a new constraint is redundant is: <math>\pi_{m} = 1 - \frac{2\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}{{m-1}\choose i}}{\sum_{i=0}^{d}{m\choose i}}</math>. (Note: <math>\lim_{m \to \infty}{\pi_m} = 1</math>, and as we add more constraints, the probability a new constraint is redundant approaches 100%).<ref name=":1" />
* The expected number of non-redundant constraints is: <math>C_d(m) = \frac{2m\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}{{m-1}\choose i}}{\sum_{i=0}^{d}{{m}\choose i}}</math>. (Note: <math>\lim_{m \to \infty}C_d(m) = 2d</math>).<ref name=":1" />

== Example uses ==

* Minimal caps
* [[Macbeath region]]s
* Approximations (approximations of convex bodies see properties of definition 1)
* Economic cap covering theorem (see relation from properties of definition 1 to floating bodies)
